why: Detecting a loop means reading one session's output across time and recognising repetition; no harness distinguishes a wedged agent from a productive one, and both keep emitting, so a user would have to sit and watch or scroll back. Across 3-12 sessions nobody does this reliably. Payoff is directly in saved budget and hours.

An ordered queue requires knowing every session's state at once and ranking them; no harness shows anything about other sessions, so the honest answer is cycling tabs and remembering, which produces recency order not priority order. Having it right changes which tab you go to next, many times a day.

I would literally count my terminal tabs, or run tmux list-panes or ps. That is one command in a place I know. The item itself states no decision is attached: knowing the number 7 rather than 6 changes nothing I do.

Doing this by hand today means stopping the session, commissioning workflow scaffolding, and re-briefing the agent with the context it already had; possible but a deliberate multi-minute detour, not 30 seconds. Impact is real but narrow: it only pays off for the subset of users already running structured workflows.

A dead session is fairly visible in its own pane: shell prompt returned, or ps shows nothing. But you must check each pane, and a hung-but-alive process looks the same as a working one, so it is several places plus some ambiguity rather than one glance. Payoff is not sitting waiting on a corpse, worth real minutes but rarely lost work.

In a Claude session I type /usage and get the quota picture, and Barista-style status lines surface it unprompted; the per-model split is roughly there, for that one session. So it is one command in a known place. Impact is high because it converts a hard stop into a model switch and keeps me working.

Nothing warns me the wall is coming with enough lead time to act; I would have to watch /context or /usage myself and then hand-write a handoff at the right moment, which nobody does reliably. When it is missed you lose the session's accumulated context and re-explain everything, which is concrete lost time.

Token output rate over time is nowhere on screen; reconstructing it means sampling a session repeatedly or parsing session files, which is correlating across time and no normal user does it. But the item admits no decision is attached: a pretty rate curve does not change what I type next.

I can scroll back to the plan the agent wrote and run git status and git diff to see what it actually touched: two known places plus manual comparison, so reachable but definitely not 30 seconds, and I have to do it per session. Catching scope drift early prevents a review-time unwind, a real decision I make regularly.

The blocking prompt is fully visible in its own pane, and Claude Desktop even shows indicator dots, so per session this is a glance; the cost is that I must visit every pane to find which one is waiting. That is tedium across several places, so mid. Impact is the highest in the set: an unnoticed prompt means the session sits idle for however long I look away.
